source: Liu, Geng, Wu, Sucholutsky, Lombrozo, Griffiths (2025, ICML) Mind Your Step (by Step): Chain-of-Thought can Reduce Performance on Tasks where Thinking Makes Humans Worse
finding: Gap 5 and 7. Forcing chain of thought on an artificial grammar learning task (the classic implicit learning task, as in Fallshore and Schooler 1993) lowers accuracy for most LLMs. A forced verbal reasoning step hurts where the structure is hard to state.
numbers: AGL, 50% chance. GPT-4o 87.50 direct vs 64.40 CoT (-23.1 pts, p<.0001); Claude 3 Opus 70.70 vs 62.70; Gemini 1.5 Pro 68.00 vs 61.95; Llama 3.1 70B 65.90 vs 57.10; Claude 3.5 Sonnet 65.90 vs 67.70 (no drop, p=.969); small Llamas -1.8 to -2.2. o1-preview on a 440-item subset: 57.70 vs GPT-4o direct 94.00 (-36.3 pts). Temperature 0 to 0.7: GPT-4o direct 87.5-88.3, CoT 63.6-64.4.
quote: CoT greatly reduces performance in a majority of models
limits: Direct-answer comparison is not token matched (CoT uses far more tokens). o1 cannot have its reasoning removed, so GPT-4o direct is the comparator. 100 grammars (6-node finite state grammar). Not every model drops.
agent_relevance: Do not add a forced 'state the rule' step to pattern-judgement items; keep a direct-answer path for statistical or perceptual tasks. Supports the guardrail against forced verbalisation.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Mind Your Step, in-context steering and tree-of-thought controls (Appendix A.4, A.7)
finding: Telling the model which strategy suits the task (use bigram patterns) only partly repairs the CoT loss; tree-of-thought does not repair it either.
numbers: GPT-4o AGL subset: zero-shot 94.00, CoT 62.52, ToT 64.55; bigram steering 68.43 vs zero-shot 87.50 and CoT 64.40 (440-item subset).
limits: ToT run on only 10 grammars. Single model.
agent_relevance: Even a correct hint to the explicit step does not recover implicit performance: the explicit route itself is the cost.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Mind Your Step, exceptions task (replicates the Williams, Lombrozo, Rehder 2013 deliberation effect) and face recognition (verbal overshadowing analogue)
finding: Two more human 'thinking hurts' effects appear in LLMs: face recognition after describing faces (analogue of Schooler and Engstler-Schooler 1990) and learning labels when a rule has exceptions.
numbers: Face recognition (5 choices, chance 20%): GPT-4o 64.00 direct vs 51.20 CoT (-12.8); Claude 3 Opus 44.00 vs 29.60 (-14.4); Gemini 1.5 Pro 66.00 vs 54.60; Claude 3.5 Sonnet 97.80 vs 94.80 (-3.0). Exceptions task (240 lists, up to 15 passes): GPT-4o needs 2.9 passes direct vs 12.5 with CoT (+331%, p<.0001); Claude 3.5 Sonnet 2.3 vs 6.4.
limits: Synthetic generated faces, no distractor delay. Task transfer from human to model is imperfect (the paper also reports tasks where the human pattern did not carry over).
agent_relevance: Matches CLARION's claim that explicit hypothesis testing slows learning on non-salient structure. Gap 5 closes for LLMs: forced rule-finding hurts on these task types, with model-by-model variation.

source: Alogna et al. (2014) Registered Replication Report: Schooler and Engstler-Schooler (1990). Perspectives on Psychological Science 9(5)
finding: Gap 7 (human side, lineup version). Verbal overshadowing replicates but much smaller than the original when the description comes right after the event (RRR1), and about as large as the original in RRR2. Task order (description immediately after the event, or after a delay and filler) was the moderator.
numbers: Original: 22% difference (RRR1 order) and 25.00% (RRR2 order) fewer correct lineup picks after describing the robber. RRR1: 31 labs, meta-analytic -4.01% [95% CI -7.15 to -0.87], heterogeneity at chance (I2=0, Tau=0). RRR2: 22 labs, -16.31% [-20.47 to -12.14].
quote: the verbal overshadowing effect is smaller with a delay between the description and lineup task
limits: Faces, not insight problems. RRR1 protocol had a task-order error that the authors found and fixed in RRR2. The effect is real but timing-sensitive.
agent_relevance: Verbal-interference effects are real but moderated by timing. Expect an LLM version to be moderated too (see d01 to d03). This does not test Schooler 1993 insight narration.

source: Alogna et al. (2014) RRR design notes (same paper, methods section, submitted manuscript)
finding: Pre-registered multi-lab design; one lab also ran an online Mechanical Turk version of both task orders.
numbers: Minimum 50 participants per condition per lab; undergraduates aged 18-25; 31 labs joined, 22 completed RRR2. RRR1 individual-lab estimates ranged about 17.54 to 14.00 points in magnitude (signs lost in text extraction).
limits: Read is the submitted manuscript version, not the published PDF.
agent_relevance: Larger-N answer for the face version of gap 7. No registered replication of the Schooler 1993 insight-narration result was found in the sources opened.

source: Lee et al. (2026, Findings of EMNLP) DART: Draft-Agreement Routing for Training-Free Adaptive Thinking Budgets in Hybrid Reasoning Models
finding: Gap 1 and 2. A fast-default, escalate-on-disagreement router (two cheap no-think drafts, accept if they agree, else think with an entropy-set budget) matches always-thinking accuracy on 13 of 14 model-benchmark pairs with 32-73% fewer thinking tokens. Independent group from SOFAI and SwiftSage.
numbers: Qwen3-8B: MATH-500 NT 76.6, always-think (AT) 85.6, DART 88.2 (35% fewer total tokens); OlympiadBench NT 49.8, AT 71.5, DART 69.8 (9% fewer); HumanEval NT 60.4, AT 59.1, DART 78.7 (52% fewer). McNemar vs AT: p=.066 MATH-500, p=.30 Olympiad (not distinguishable). Majority vote of 3-7 no-think drafts: 82.4-84.8 on MATH-500 but about 10 on HumanEval.
quote: preserves or improves always-thinking accuracy in most settings while reducing thinking-token use
limits: Savings are in emitted tokens versus always-think, not an equal-token accuracy comparison. Math and code only. Always-think baseline uses a two-phase protocol to avoid truncation.
agent_relevance: Independent support that fast-default plus escalate-on-disagreement is not worse than always-slow, at fewer tokens. Disagreement between two cheap samples is a usable escalation trigger.

source: Lee et al. (2026) DART, routing baselines (Table 2) and self-reported confidence routing
finding: Gap 9. Routing from the model's self-reported confidence (MC-Conf) does worse than draft agreement; supervised routers trained on entropy and length also trail.
numbers: Qwen3-8B: MC-Conf MATH-500 85.8 (24% fewer tokens), OlympiadBench 54.9 (AT 71.5), HumanEval 8.5; MC-Binary HumanEval 10.4; DART 88.2 / 69.8 / 78.7. Supervised MLP: 81.0 / 58.2 / 62.5.
limits: Compares routers, not final-answer weighting. The collapse to about 10% on HumanEval for the vote and self-prompt rows looks partly like a format artefact; the authors attribute it to needing execution-based agreement.
agent_relevance: Felt confidence is a weak trigger; use disagreement or an executable check. Partial answer to gap 9 (routing, not selection).

source: Ma et al. (2026) ODAR: Principled Adaptive Routing for LLM Reasoning via Active Inference
finding: Gap 1. Difficulty-routed fast and slow agents beat a proportion-matched random router at the same call budget, and beat self-consistency at lower cost, across 23 benchmarks.
numbers: Average 89.6% vs self-consistency 83.6% (+6.0); cost 0.42 vs 0.75 (1.78x lower). Learned routing beats proportion-matched randomized routing by +8.3 macro points (same 41/35/24% path mix and token limits). Macro averages: single model 77.6, rules-only 79.2, router with heuristics off 88.4, full 89.6.
limits: Single group, proprietary models (GPT-5.1 fast, Claude 4.5 slow). A fusion step also contributes. Fast agent 512 tokens, slow 1024 tokens. Unreplicated.
agent_relevance: Closest token-matched control found: the gain comes from choosing which items get slow thinking, not from extra calls. Still self-reported.

source: Sprague et al. (2025, ICLR) To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning
finding: Gap 1 and 2. Meta-analysis of over 100 papers plus 20 datasets by 14 models: CoT helps on math, symbolic and logic tasks and barely elsewhere. About 95% of the MMLU gain comes from questions with an equals sign. A plan-then-tool-solver beats CoT for both steps on GSM8K-Hard, ContextHub and FOLIO.
numbers: Average CoT gain over direct: symbolic 14.2, math 12.3, logical 6.9 points. Top three categories 56.9 with CoT vs 45.5 without; other categories 56.8 vs 56.1.
quote: CoT gives strong performance benefits primarily on tasks involving math or logic
limits: Authors note CoT uses more compute and a fair test would match compute. Unparseable plans are scored as a random guess or wrong, so solver routes carry a parse-failure cost.
agent_relevance: Gives a per-item route rule: formalise and solve when the task is symbolic or arithmetic; skip CoT elsewhere. Explains why Logic-LM can lose on PrOntoQA (CoT already near ceiling, translation adds failure points).

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2024) On the Self-Verification Limitations of Large Language Models on Reasoning and Planning Tasks
finding: Gap 3. A validate layer helps only if the verifier is sound. GPT-4 as its own verifier makes results worse; a sound external verifier gives large gains, and merely resampling keeps much of the gain.
numbers: 100 instances per domain, accuracy: Game of 24 standard 5%, LLM+LLM 3%, sound verifier 36-38%, sampling k=15 28%, k=25 42%. Graph colouring 16 / 2 / 34-38 / 40-44. Blocksworld 40 / 55 / 60-87 / 68-72. Mystery Blocksworld 4 / 0 / 6-10 / 9-14. LLM verifier false negative rates 95.8% (graph colouring) and 97.09% (mystery blocks).
limits: GPT-4 only, 100 instances per domain, early-2024 model. Reasoning models may verify better.
agent_relevance: An explicit veto only helps when it is sound (code, solver, test). An LLM veto layer mostly rejects correct answers. Gap 3 answered: measured negative for LLM self-veto, positive for sound external veto.

source: Huang et al. (2024, ICLR) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Gap 3. Self-correction gains in prior work came from oracle labels. Without oracle labels, intrinsic self-correction lowers accuracy.
numbers: GPT-3.5 with oracle: GSM8K 75.9 to 95.5, HotpotQA 26.0 to 49.0 (GPT-4 oracle: 97.5, 59.0). Intrinsic: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 74.7 after two rounds; CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 (round 1) and 41.8; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0. GPT-3.5 keeps its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time and, when it changes, more often goes right to wrong than wrong to right. Multi-agent debate no better than self-consistency at equal calls (6 calls: 83.2 vs 85.3).
quote: improvements vanish when oracle labels are not available
limits: 2023 models; 100-question samples for some tasks. Later reasoning models may differ.
agent_relevance: A veto with no ground truth hurts. Give the verifier real information (tests, tools, retrieved facts), not a second opinion from the same model.

source: Zhu et al. (2024) Large Language Models can Learn Rules (Hypotheses-to-Theories, HtT)
finding: Gap 4. Bottom-up rule extraction works if rules are filtered: an LLM proposes rules on 2,000 training examples, rules with enough coverage and confidence are kept in a library, and later answers improve. Random wrong rules are very harmful.
numbers: CLUTRR symbolic, 5-shot CoT: GPT-3.5 21.2 to 37.6 (+16.4); with rules induced by GPT-4, 48.4 (+27.2); GPT-4 50.6 to 64.3 (+13.7). Base-16 arithmetic GPT-4 57.4 to 78.4 (+21.0). Incorrect rules were 65% (CLUTRR) and 81% (base-16) of CoT errors. Replacing rule conclusions with random answers: GPT-4 CLUTRR 9.9 (-40.7), arithmetic 23.7 (-33.7). Textual CLUTRR GPT-3.5 only +0.3.
limits: Fixed rule types (kinship, arithmetic, list functions); rules are checked against training labels before use. 200 CLUTRR test items. Library must fit in context.
agent_relevance: Direct measured analogue of CLARION-style rule extraction. The coverage and confidence filter guards against cascading wrong rules; an unfiltered wrong rule does more harm than no rule.

source: Zabounidis et al. (2026) SCALAR: Learning and Composing Skills through LLM Guided Symbolic Planning and Deep RL Grounding
finding: Gap 4 and 8. An LLM writes explicit skill specifications (preconditions and effects), RL trains implicit policies, and RL trajectories feed back to correct the specs. Explicit-top-down plus implicit-bottom-up correction beats RL baselines. A 2026 survey (arXiv 2607.23942) lists it as the modern counterpart of CLARION cross-level learning; the SCALAR paper itself does not mention CLARION.
numbers: Craftax-Classic collect diamond 88.2% vs 46.9% for the best baseline (1.9x); Gnomish Mines 9.1% vs 0% for prior methods. Removing trajectory analysis: diamond 88% to 67%, Gnomish Mines 9% to 0%. After a crafting-rule change, without trajectory analysis success falls to 5.4%; with it, it recovers above 86%.
limits: One game environment (Craftax), 5 seeds. The CLARION link is the survey's reading, not the authors'.
agent_relevance: Measured evidence that correcting explicit LLM rules from implicit execution traces avoids stuck wrong rules. Supports a validate-before-commit step for stored rules.

source: Yuan et al. (2025) NL2GenSym: Natural Language to Generative Symbolic Rules for SOAR (LLM plus Soar generator-critic)
finding: Gap 8 (Soar, not Sigma). Measured LLM-plus-cognitive-architecture result: LLMs write Soar production rules from a task description and a critic loop refines them. Zero-shot rule writing fails completely.
numbers: Water jug problems, success rate: Gemini-2.5-pro one-shot 55% to NL2GenSym 86%; qwen-max one-shot 66% to 91%; manual rules 84%; zero-shot 0% for both. Hard cases (Gemini): one-shot 20% to 76.67%.
limits: One puzzle family. Authors' own baselines. Not Sigma and not the Common Model work.
agent_relevance: LLM as rule generator with a critic over a symbolic runtime works when execution feedback exists; unaided generation fails. Fits an LLM-proposes, architecture-checks split.

source: Rosenbloom, Laird, Lebiere, Stocco (2025) Mapping Neural Theories of Consciousness onto the Common Model of Cognition (arXiv 2506.12224, AGI-25)
finding: Gap 8. No measurements. A conceptual mapping of four neural consciousness theories onto the Common Model. All three Rosenbloom-group arXiv papers named in the gap (2412.16231 emotion, 2506.07807 metacognition, 2506.12224 consciousness) are proposals.
numbers: No quantitative results and no LLM tests in any of the three.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: no quantitative Sigma-with-LLM result found. The three unopened papers are now opened and are conceptual.

source: Laird, Lebiere, Rosenbloom, Stocco (2025) A Proposal to Extend the Common Model of Cognition with Metacognition (2506.07807); Rosenbloom et al. (2024) extending the Common Model to emotion (2412.16231)
finding: Metacognition is proposed as reasoning over explicit representations of the agent's own capabilities held in working memory, with minimal extension. Emotion is proposed as a linked pair of modules. In Sigma and Soar an impasse creates a substate; ACT-R lacks that.
limits: Position papers describing what ACT-R, Sigma and Soar do, not test results.
agent_relevance: Design idea that matches schema operators: self-model as explicit state, impasse-triggered sub-problem. No evidence of benefit yet.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: Gap 9. Without an automatic verifier, majority voting and a reward model stop improving after about 100 samples while coverage keeps rising. With real verifiers (unit tests, proof checker) coverage turns directly into accuracy.
numbers: MATH with Llama-3-8B-Instruct: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000; majority vote or reward-model pick only 40.50% to 41.41%. SWE-bench Lite DeepSeek-Coder-V2: 15.9% with 1 sample to 56% with 250.
limits: Compares vote and learned-reward selection, not felt confidence directly. Reward model was an 8B ArmoRM.
agent_relevance: Verifier-weighted selection scales when verification is exact; vote or score-weighted selection saturates. Indirect support for mirroring b25 in gap 9.

source: Stechly et al. (2024) self-verification, critique-content ablation (same paper, section 5)
finding: With a sound verifier, critique content matters little; plain re-prompting with a pass/fail signal gets most of the gain. LLM-written critiques contain hallucinations.
numbers: Binary vs first-error vs all-error feedback: Game of 24 36 vs 38; graph colouring 38 / 37 / 34; Blocksworld 60 / 87 / 83. Resampling with the sound check but no critique text (k=25) reaches 42 (Game of 24), 44 (graph colouring), 72 (Blocksworld).
agent_relevance: Spend tokens on more attempts gated by an exact check, not on long critiques.

source: Search status note, gap 6: independent CLARION model fits
finding: No independent-group replication of CLARION fits (process control, serial reaction time) and no reported fit statistics were found. The shared WebSearch budget ran out and the arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex APIs returned 429 or empty during this pass.
limits: Absence of evidence in this session only, not proof that none exists.
agent_relevance: Treat CLARION human-data fits as single-group until shown otherwise.
